interactions.summary: Jiang restates Purgatory as a discipline that strips away material desire so the soul can recover its relation to the good.
A student reads Dante's request that Virgil define love and Virgil's answer that love is the soul's movement toward what beauty awakens.
Jiang condenses the exchange into a stark premise: love is the universe's fundamental force and its direction determines whether action becomes good or bad.
Jiang interprets love as a confused embodied drive to possess beauty, using Dido's fixation on Aeneas as the example of the soul trying to consume what it finds beautiful.
The reading complicates the account by rejecting the idea that every love is praiseworthy and by raising the problem of merit if the soul is moved from without.

claims.claim: Jiang says the purpose of Purgatory is to cleanse material wants so the soul can remember its origin and reconnect to the good before entering heaven.
Jiang frames love as the fundamental force of the universe, with moral difference arising from whether we move toward or away from it.
Virgil's definition, as read in class, says love is the soul's natural propulsion toward what pleases it, just as fire rises toward its proper sphere.
Jiang interprets the soul as a memory of God trapped in a body, trying to return to the divine but getting confused by beautiful worldly objects.
Jiang says confused desire does not merely admire beauty but expands outward to absorb, control, and consume it.
Jiang uses Dido's relation to Aeneas as the paradigm of consuming love: desire mistakes possession for fulfillment and becomes destructive when the object withdraws.
The quoted passage rejects the thesis that every love is praiseworthy and raises the problem of how blame or merit are possible if love comes from outside the soul.
Virgil's answer in this packet is incomplete on purpose: he can explain only what reason sees, and the fuller answer belongs to Beatrice and faith.

signature_moments.moment: Love is pictured as a firelike motion of the soul, rising toward what seems to belong to its own sphere.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It provides the packet's core image for desire as motion rather than sentiment.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns desire into a swallowing movement: the soul reaches toward beauty and tries to consume it whole.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's sharpest formulation of possessive love and sets up the later free-will problem.

signature_moments.moment: The text refuses to sanctify love automatically: the wax may be good while the seal impressed into it is not.

signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves Dante's distinction between the underlying power of love and its morally distorted forms.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Virgil's image for love as the soul's restless movement toward what beauty awakens.
Jiang's phrase for the soul's divine origin, which explains why it longs to return upward even while embodied confusion misdirects it.
Jiang's account of desire as an attempt to possess and control beauty rather than give oneself to it.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-05-22 lecture stages the free-will problem in sequence: Jiang first defines love as the universe's basic force and consuming movement, then leaves the explicit answer to the next packet via Virgil's deferral to Beatrice.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang says Dido sees Aeneas 'in the Iliad,' which is likely a lecture slip or transcript drift; the packet preserves the possessive-love example without normalizing the classical reference.
